The Stage of Wisdom Accomplished through Cultivation (18b). Treatise, Main Body, Section 67, Sub-section 9:
Determination of the Stage of Wisdom Accomplished through Cultivation. Within this, first, the preceding section is concluded and the subsequent section is introduced; next...
After the correct discernment (*samyag-viniścaya*), the remainder does not appear.
Within the section on correct discernment, sixteen types of names are first listed,
which will subsequently be explained in order.
In the *Zhongjing* (Middle Scripture) on the cultivation of the Śrāvaka vehicle, it says:
"Regarding the statement that one internally contemplates suchness by means of the mental application (*manasikāra*) of the established truths (*vyavasthāpita-satya*),
this refers to contemplating the four truths as a whole, taking the realization of the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*) as the gateway."
One enters into the realization of suchness.
This takes the ultimate truth as its object;
that which takes finite and conceptual phenomena as its objective referent [is not so].
This refers to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Knowing that objects have limits is called "having measure" (*sopamāna*).
Not being free from attachment to phenomena (*dharma-abhiniveśa*) is called "having conceptual differentiation" (*savikalpa*).
Now, the explanation of this consists of five points:
first, abiding in the lineage;
second, the stage of discerning practice.
"Those who have not yet entered the state of right determination" refers to the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya*).
"Those who have already entered the state of right determination" refers to those from the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) onwards.
Third, regarding the cultivation of mental action (*manaskarma*), it seeks only self-benefit.
Fourth is the exposition of the gate of contemplation:
although at the time of direct realization the objects are non-conceptually established (*apratiṣṭhita*),
when first practicing the preparatory means, one must necessarily contemplate the Four Noble Truths.
Therefore, it is said that by way of the door of formal establishment,
correct wisdom directly realizes the principle of signless emptiness;
thus, it is said that one internally contemplates suchness.
Subsequent knowledge takes conventional reality as its object and possesses distinctions with limits;
therefore, it is called "discrimination that takes the finite as its object.
Fifth, the explanation of what is accomplished begins with the passage: "Having exhausted craving and attachment," and so forth.
Regarding those who practice the Mahāyāna and those who are progressing toward the supreme track:
"track" refers to the path traversed by the former sages, namely bodhi and nirvāṇa;
those who are currently progressing toward these are [the ones referred to].
The old [translation] says "Unsurpassed Way.
It is that which is traversed and dwelled upon by those whose Way is complete.
Regarding this, Xingyuan (Xingjing) said: [text follows].
Investigation by means of cognitive nature is called "with conceptual differentiation.
That which shares the same object as meditative concentration is called "the range of samādhi.
The tranquility of the concentrated mind is called "without conceptual differentiation."
Tai says:
"The 'image' refers to the color-form within the meditative state that resembles external color-form; it is called an 'image' because it appears like something outside of meditation.
The fundamental colors such as blue, yellow, and so forth within meditation are termed the 'objects of knowledge' (*jñeya-vastu*)."
Because the determined colors such as blue and yellow resemble external colors, they are called "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*).
Because they are similar, they are of the same class (*nikāya-sabhāga*).
Both *samādhi* and *prajñā* are termed *samādhi*.
Regarding the "limit of phenomena" (*vastuparyanta*):
based on this text, knowing things exhaustively according to convention is called the "nature of all that exists" (*yāvadbhāvikatā*);
illuminating them in accordance with reality is called the "nature of suchness" (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*).
The old [translation] states that "knowing according to principle and according to measure" refers to knowing the objects of principle.
Regarding the attainment of cultivation (*bhāvanā-lābha*), according to the Abhidharma, there is the prior attainment of dharmas;
one attains future dharmas as belonging to oneself.
The cultivation that consists in the actualization of what has not yet arisen is called "cultivation by attainment" (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*).
Now, within the Mahāyāna, as in the case of the ten perceptions (*daśasaṃjñā*),
the actualization of any one perception induces all the other perceptions that are not currently manifest.
It is called "cultivation through acquisition" (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*) because it causes the seeds to flourish and reach mastery in their maturation; or,
it refers to the manifestation of any one of the practices belonging to its own level.
It perfumes and causes the seeds of one's own and lower-level practices to increase;
this is also "cultivation through attainment" (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*).
Alternatively, it refers to the manifestation of mundane practices.
Abhijñā (supernormal power) is able to induce the seeds of mundane and supramundane practices to increase;
this refers to the case of noble beings (*ārya*).
Alternatively, it refers to the manifestation of supramundane dharmas through abhijñā.
It is capable of inducing the mundane and supramundane seeds and causing them to increase and excel;
that is to say, upon entering the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one cultivates those seven types of preparatory means (*prayoga*) so that they increase,
which is termed the "retinue of the path of seeing."
Arising within the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanāvasthā*) is not termed "factors conducive to liberation" (*mokṣabhāgīya*) and so forth.

As for "cultivation through practice" (*abhyāsa-bhāvanā*), it refers to the repeated manifestation of a single path, such as the perception of impermanence (*anityasaṃjñā*), or the cultivation of other wholesome dharmas when they manifest; this is also called cultivation through practice.
Regarding the statement that "the practitioner removes [impurities] by contemplating the impurity of the body,
and employs the skillful means of extracting a wedge with a wedge to dispel the appearance of pure signs before them": this refers to the following.
This is because there are many varieties of mental attention (*manasikāra*) cultivated in meditative concentration; thus,
the characteristics of the objects of focus (*ālambana-nimitta*) also possess degrees of coarseness and subtlety,
as subsequent mental attentions gradually abandon and discard the preceding coarse ones.
Regarding the statement that "the body of pliancy removes the body of coarse heaviness":
because the pliancy of the form realm resides within the body,
it causes the practitioner’s body to become supple and removes the seeds of the desire realm.
Because the seeds of *dauṣṭhulya* (coarseness) cause the body to become coarse, they must be eliminated.
Within the cultivation of remedies (*pratipakṣabhāvanā*),
the remedy of revulsion (*vidūṣaṇā-pratipakṣa*) refers to all mundane wholesome paths, excluding the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) and the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
It is removed by means of the antidote of non-disgust.
As for the antidote of maintenance, this refers to the subsequently attained mundane and supramundane paths, as well as the path of liberation;
regarding this, there are two interpretations.
One interpretation states:
This passage acknowledges that non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) serves as the antidote of abandonment (*prahāṇa-pratipakṣa*),
while subsequent wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) serves as the antidote of liberation (*vimukti-pratipakṣa*), which is so named because it externally manifests the removal of obscurations.
The second says:
This refers to those who possess the subsequently attained mundane and supramundane paths;
it takes this subsequent knowledge as the path of liberation.
This [system] takes non-conceptual wisdom as the fruit of liberation and employs a single wisdom as the path to liberation;
although there are two types of liberation, the latter is superior.
Furthermore, there is a distinction:
those who call the paths of hearing, reflection, and cultivation "disgust" (udvega) mean that the practice of the three types of wisdom (prajñā) encompasses both aspiration and disgust.
Now, taking the practice of revulsion as "the antidote of aversion," and its result,
the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), as "the sustaining antidote" (*dhāraṇa-pratipakṣa*),
there are two interpretations of this.
One interpretation states that this fruit of the path of non-obstruction is the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
Since this path of liberation is that which can realize the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*),
this fruit is called the "transformation of the basis" and is termed the "retention of the antidote" (*pratipakṣa-dhāraṇa*).
The second [master] says:
That which takes up the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) transformation of the basis (āśrayaparāvṛtti), whether as that which can maintain [the state] or as non-arising,
is called the "maintaining antidote" (dhāraṇa-pratipakṣa).
Regarding these, the four types of cultivation are the same as the four types of cultivation discussed in the previous fascicle;
one should examine them to determine whether they are identical or distinct.
"Cultivation of a limited portion" refers to the cultivation arising from contemplating a single characteristic, such as impermanence.
The universal cultivation consists in contemplating all phenomena as they truly are.
The cultivated cultivation with effort occurs at the time of practicing the skillful means of the non-conceptual cultivation;
it is so called because spontaneous cultivation has not yet been attained.
10. Śrāvaka-bhūmi (18b–19a). Within the twelve sections of the subsequent *viniścaya* portion of the *Śrāvaka-bhūmi*, nine sections have been explained.
From here below is the tenth section, which provides a definitive resolution regarding the Śrāvaka-bhūmi and the Pratyekabuddha-bhūmi; it consists of four and a half fascicles.
Within this, only the Śrāvaka-bhūmi is definitively resolved, while the Pratyekabuddha-bhūmi is not.
This section is divided into three parts:
first, connecting the preceding with the subsequent;
second, the actual determination; and third, concluding with the non-manifestation [of the remainder].
However, within the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī*, there is first an analysis by means of seven gates;
next, an analysis by means of thirteen gates through a single verse;
and finally, an extensive analysis through sixty-four gates in various determinations (*viniścaya*).
At the beginning of the first section, there are five challenges regarding sentient beings who lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
In response, it is said that "various realms of nature" (*nānā-dhātu-svabhāva*) refers to various intrinsic natures,
while "immeasurable realms of nature" (*apramāṇa-dhātu-svabhāva*) refers to their immeasurable differentiation.
Regarding the statement that there are no sentient beings without roots:
it means there are no beings who lack the twenty-two faculties.
As for the question of whether this applies to all realms or whether it refers to only one realm, and so forth:

If there were other three types of sentient beings within the kṣatriya caste, or other four places and four realms of existence within the intermediate state (antarābhava), the analogy would be dissimilar;
for among those phenomena used as analogies, there is no nature of nirvāṇa.
The phrase "there is no realm of nirvāṇa" means that there is no realm of nirvāṇa.
Just as among those in the hells there may be a single individual who possesses the seed-realm of one [particular] destiny,
so too for those who lack the nature for nirvāṇa, there exists only the realm of non-nirvāṇa.
Therefore, one should know that it is impossible for someone who has been in hell to subsequently become even a śūdra.
To say that this same *pudgala* is both one who lacks the nature of parinirvāṇa and one who possesses the nature of parinirvāṇa, provided there is no contradiction, is not logical.
All sentient beings, in brief, are of two types:
first, those who are ultimately able to sever the two obstacles;
second, those who seek but are unable to sever the two obstacles.
The first person possesses the nature for parinirvāṇa;
the second person is one who lacks the dharma for parinirvāṇa.
If you claim that these two persons do not contradict one another, it is unreasonable.
Regarding the statement, "If one says it is so, then the roots of goodness conducive to liberation (mokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla) would have no fruit," Jing says:
"If that were the case, the roots of liberation previously planted would be empty and bear no fruit."
Because it would then be rendered without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
Furthermore, if that were the case, it would be indeterminate;
thus, for it to possess a determinate nature (*niyatasvabhāva*) would be irrational.
Tai said: As the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states:
"One attains the dharma of mundane right view."
In the world of the hundred sons, they shall never fall into the evil realms;
they are those who have planted the factors conducive to liberation and will certainly attain nirvana.
If one lacked the nature for nirvana, [this would not be so].
The factors conducive to liberation exist subsequent to nirvāṇa;
if one were to act as one who lacks the nature for nirvāṇa,
then the wholesome roots conducive to liberation would be empty and fruitless, and one would not attain nirvāṇa.

To say that one who has encountered the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha and is able to give rise to the roots of goodness conducive to liberation within the present life cannot attain parinirvāṇa is unreasonable.
Since one is able to give rise to the roots of goodness conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*) once one has encountered the Three Jewels,
we know that within the ālayavijñāna there exists, from time immemorial,
the seed capable of producing these roots of goodness conducive to liberation.
If one says that although there exist seeds of the roots of goodness conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*),
it is nonetheless impossible for them to attain parinirvāṇa, this is unreasonable.
However, regarding the principles of having such a nature (*gotra*) or lacking it, the sūtras and śāstras differ.

In the "Section on Refuting Attachments" (*Poxie fen*) of the *Foxing lun* (Treatise on the Buddha-nature), those who establish the existence or non-existence of nature are taken as the objects of refutation.
That [text] states:
"The Buddha taught that sentient beings exist for the sake of those of the Hīnayāna."
Because they do not abide in a fixed nature and never enter parinirvāṇa,
doubt arises regarding this, and a lack of faith is produced.
To challenge this point, he asks:

If you believe that there are various coarse and subtle realms of sentient beings, and thereby believe that there are sentient beings who lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), then you should also believe that there are those who lack sense faculties (*indriya*). Why?
Because sentient beings exist by virtue of having or lacking sense faculties.
Therefore, there are various realms, such as the coarse and the subtle.
If you do not believe that there are sentient beings without roots,
how could there be coarse and subtle realms?
If you claim that there are realms such as coarse and subtle without distinguishing between those with faculties and those without faculties,
I likewise accept the principle that there are coarse and subtle realms without distinguishing between those with intrinsic nature and those without.
What fault is there in this position?
If you say that there are no rootless sentient beings— and so forth, as extensively refuted in the section on the limits of the teachings established for the foolish—
this is not something to be measured by those who look with two eyes [i.e., biased perspectives].
Second, the differentiation of the śrāvakas is divided into two parts:
first, the differentiation of ten types, and second, the differentiation of two categories.
Within the former, it says that "those who have already entered the Dharma" are called the second.
This refers to those śrāvakas who have already planted the roots of goodness conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*).
Regarding the term "śrāvaka-gate of the pure realm," such individuals are born in a pure land;
alternatively, they may also be born during a period when the world is in a state of flourishing.
Regarding "such as when Maitreya appears," and the phrase "being stingy toward a stingy household and so forth":
if one follows the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* (*Satyasiddhi-śāstra*) to clarify its five types of stinginess.
That is to say: stinginess regarding dwellings,
stinginess regarding families,
and stinginess regarding giving.
This praises the stinginess of the Dharma (*dharmamātsarya*). Herein,
six types are distinguished to show their differences.
Regarding the statement that "the bedding for the limit has three grades," this refers to the lowest grade, and is therefore called the "limit.
Regarding the statement "without the other two categories of grave offenses":
The first section is exhaustive (without remainder),
while the second section is non-exhaustive (with remainder).
As for the term "Saṃghika," it is translated here as "the assembly" (saṃgha).
Regarding the "time of excellence and goodness," there are two interpretations.
One is that the period of the True Dharma (Saddharma) and the Semblance Dharma (Pratirūpakadharma) is called the time of excellence and goodness.
Another says that only the period of the True Dharma is called the time of excellence and goodness.
Regarding the statement "all [arose] because they had not yet arisen":
this means that when the Tathāgata first appeared in the world, there was as yet no breaking of the precepts or of right view;
it was only later that Sudinna first violated the full set of monastic vows.
Āḷavaka was the first to refute the view that desire does not obstruct the Middle Way;
in this context, refuting such views is termed "self-completion.
It is said that there are some who, after attaining parinirvāṇa, undergo such manifold bodily disintegrations at the end of life and yet again attain rebirth in auspicious realms, and so forth.
There are some individuals in their final birth who,
having encountered a virtuous person after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, for the most part pass away and are reborn in a happy realm; yet,
having later committed evil deeds, they are for a small portion of time reborn in an evil realm.
All of these are virtuous people of the present age.
The following clarifies two categories: the slow and the swift.
First, there are those who exert themselves in the Path but lack the power of cultivation, and therefore do not enter the Noble Path.
Second, because they are negligent, although they possess the power of cultivation, they have not yet entered the Noble Path.
Third, the *Candropama-sūtra* explains the four dharmas beginning with perfect ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Regarding the "four kinds of purity," these refer to faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, and ethical discipline.

Fourth, when a śrāvaka intends to visit another's household, he should first eliminate three secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). Regarding the statement that "one should sever the secondary afflictions associated with visiting the households of kinsmen and friends through six modes of application": [it refers to the following: 1. The secondary affliction of attachment to the household; 2. The secondary affliction of attachment to the person; 3. The secondary affliction of attachment to the objects of enjoyment;

4. The secondary affliction of attachment to the requisites; 5. The secondary affliction of attachment to the dwelling; 6. The secondary affliction of attachment to the company of others. By means of these six modes of application, one should sever these secondary afflictions. Thus it is said.
That is to say: first, approaching those who do not follow the Dharma;
second, being base regarding desirable things;
and third, being base through violence.
"Skillfully guarding oneself" is the fourth;
"furthermore, by following the mind of detachment" is the fifth;
"like a mountain" is the sixth.
Furthermore, there are six aspects by which one should abandon the stinginess of a householder:
first, not being attached to sentient beings;
second, not being attached to gain and offerings.
Third, not being attached to honor;
fourth, not giving rise to sorrow or suffering when lacking profit;
fifth, not giving rise to sorrow or suffering when not being respected.
Sixth, one maintains an even mind regarding gain and honor from oneself and others, neither praising oneself nor disparaging others.
Furthermore, there are six factors associated with the giving of the Dharma that eliminate defiled states of mind.
First, not desiring that others have pure faith in oneself;
second, knowing the dharma of renunciation as it truly is;
third, because of the induction of happiness.
Fourth, because it eliminates suffering;
fifth, because one attains great benefit through hearing the Dharma and practicing it;
sixth, because it upholds the Dharma so as to bring about liberation from suffering.
The fifth is the *Vaidika-sūtra*.
The Tripiṭaka Master says that "person" (*pudgala*) refers to one who is a native of the country of Vaidika.
The title of the sutra is established based on its subject matter.
Jingyun states:
"Vādika" is translated here as "discourse."
Because this person is capable of discourse, he is named after his speech.
Within the text, there are two parts:
first, the three chapters are opened and set forth for explanation.
The second section provides a detailed analysis.
Within the first part, it asks:
"What is the basis for affliction and purification, up to the basis for purification?"
This clarifies that for ordinary beings and those still in training, the bodies upon which their latent dispositions (anuśaya) depend all possess coarseness (dauṣṭhulya).
Here, only the supporting body is taken, not that which depends upon it.
The two subsequent gates concern the defiled and the pure states that depend [upon the basis].
Regarding the question, "What is purification... until one attains complete dissociation from all bonds?
Jing says:
The intent here is to clarify that the defilements of ordinary beings and the untainted [states] of those in training all depend upon the tainted body of coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*);
therefore, within the context of purification, only the two types of training are explained.
First, regarding the practitioner: taking the wisdom of *tathatā* (suchness) as the basis, one is able to perform actions.

Relying upon realized wisdom (*adhigama-jñāna*), one gives rise to subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) to cultivate various practices and advance in training; this is called "learning" (*śikṣā*).
This refers to the three preceding fruits of learning and to those on the ten stages.
Regarding the second type of learner, it means one who has attained dissociation from all afflictions;
that is to say, one who has severed all afflictions and realized the cultivation of non-conceptual wisdom.
Non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) is the second study;
it likewise pertains to the studies and exists throughout the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
The Dharma Master Xuan of Silla said:
The first type of practitioner refers to the bodhisattva;
the second type of practitioner refers to those of the two vehicles.
Below this, there is a further detailed analysis.
First, one explains purity and defilement, and subsequently, the basis.
Regarding the former, it says:
"This very purity is briefly revealed by five causes," and so forth; these are the five.
The causes are also pure. Among these five causes,
the afflictions abandoned through the fourth, the training in mind (*citta-śikṣā*),
and the afflictions abandoned through the fifth, the training in wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*), constitute defilement (*saṃkleśa*).
Regarding the statement "discriminative craving for what has been relinquished in accordance with the training":
one who abandons the precepts is said to have "relinquished the training.
At the time of relinquishing the training, one discriminatively craves this very act in accordance with one's own inclinations.
The *Vyākhyāyukti* states:
"The assembly of śrāvakas should thoroughly understand [the person] by means of three characteristics. First, by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*):
this refers to the intrinsic nature possessed by this human body, which is manifested through two aspects."
First, that which reveals the common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of all other bodies by virtue of being material:
it is called a "common characteristic" because it possesses materiality in common with all sentient beings.
Second, that which reveals the individual characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of each specific body by virtue of its coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*).
The individual characteristic of the body consists of the afflictions, coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*), and lack of pliancy that exist separately within each of one's own five aggregates.
Third, by virtue of being impure, it manifests as a characteristic of dissimilarity with the celestial body.
The celestial body is pure like the light of a lamp.
Second, regarding the causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), there are also three types.

First, the common causal condition of all bodies consists of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*); within the distinct individual characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of each, the causal condition for the human body is divided into two.
The preceding [section] constitutes three [parts].
The faults and defects therein are twofold,
as stated in the text.
The sixth section further clarifies the determination of the stage of wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā-bhūmi-viniścaya*), titled "Illuminating All Verses.
Within this text, the verses are cited as the question, followed by the answer.
In the answer, four causes are first presented in summary to explain and clarify the meaning.
Later, he cites a sutra as proof.
In the middle section, Jing says:
"That is to say, if one speaks briefly, it is because one contemplates the cause of purity."
Because wisdom observes that the two names are the root, one realizes the two kinds of emptiness; this is called the cause of purification.
This is because one contemplates their own characteristics as being merely the names of the four aggregates and the sounds of speech.
Regarding the observation of the causes of affliction: through the wisdom of observation, one realizes that birth and death are accumulated due to delusion regarding two kinds of names;

furthermore, in order to demonstrate the two kinds of selflessness, one thoroughly understands the selflessness of persons and so forth, up to the point where [the name] "that which eclipses all" is attained.
Delusion regarding the four aggregates consists in grasping at them as a self;
these four aggregates are collectively capable of being grasped.
If one knows that there are only the four aggregates and that they are fundamentally not the self, [then delusion is abandoned].
It is able to eliminate the objective characteristics of the grasped self.
One understands that the designation of the four aggregates eclipses all objective characteristics of what is spoken of as "self.
If one thoroughly understands that phenomena are without self and so forth, up to the point where the name eclipses everything.
Based on following verbal designations, one grasps at the existence of various phenomena (*dharma*).
If one knows that there are only names and that one grasps at phenomena according to those names,
one will ultimately and thoroughly realize that these verbal designations and names obscure all imputed phenomena and self.
Because one first conceives of a self by means of grasping at phenomena,
it is said that the grasping at phenomena is the characteristic of the basis;
namelessness subsumes all things.
If one is deluded regarding these two names, one gives rise to dualistic grasping;
these two names also obscure the principle of emptiness, and thus they are said to obscure all things.
Now, by awakening to these two names, one realizes the non-existence of the two selves.
It outshines all dualistic attachments and inversions.
The explanation of the first phrase is now complete.
As for the second phrase, "there is no name of transgression," which follows the four formless aggregates, it is explained below.
"If one does not understand both of these two types," and so forth, explains the second half of the verse: "therefore, all phenomena follow at will.
Tái says: "Yìng means to seize or to overpower."
By means of the four aggregates, one is able to sever the person-self within the objective sphere of all four aggregates;
this is called realizing the principle of the selflessness of persons.
This is because the four aggregates, being devoid of self, eclipse the characteristics of the person-self.
The statement "the name reflects all [aspects of] the self" is further explained as follows:
sentient beings mostly conceive of a self within the four aggregates.
Observing that there are only the four aggregates (*skandha*) and not perceiving a person or a self (*ātman*),
one uses the name "aggregates" to eclipse all notions of self.
Due to verbal designations, one falsely imagines that everything possesses an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
If one contemplates that there is only verbal expression and does not perceive the substantiality of phenomena, this is called "expounding the principle of the selflessness of phenomena.
Verbal expression is said to eclipse the "self of phenomena" (*dharma-ātman*).
The previous explanation of the four aggregates as eclipsing the "self of persons" (*pudgala-ātman*) was likewise intended.
Since the two names are distinct, their corresponding objects are also separate.
The following passage from the sūtra provides scriptural proof:
"Because one clings to the self-nature of phenomena, one proceeds by clinging to the nature of a self."
Due to delusion regarding words and names, one grasps at the intrinsic nature of phenomena;
only then does one proceed to delude oneself regarding the four aggregates by grasping at a self-nature.
To awaken to this is to awaken to that.
To realize that phenomena lack intrinsic nature and to realize that self and other are non-existent—
by means of this realization, one attains cessation;
by realizing the non-existence of the two selves, one brings the two views to cessation.
Seventh, the explanation of the Four Noble Truths.
First, they are presented in general terms,
referring back to what has already been said.

This refers to the fact that when entering the contemplation of suchness (*tathatā*) to sever the afflictions, one first takes the Four Noble Truths as the object of focus (*ālambana*), whether for the sake of purification or as a preliminary skillful means; thus they are called "objects of focus.
This is as explained in the *Śrāvaka-bhūmi*.
Below, the four kinds of the Four Noble Truths will be analyzed in detail.
This section is divided into three parts:
first, a general explanation of the characteristics of the truths;
second, a detailed analysis of the four truths; and third, a systematic examination of various categories.
The first passage states:
If the characteristic of truth (*satyalakṣaṇa*) were that which is non-erroneous,
then the views on truth held by the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) would all likewise be erroneous.
How are these subsumed under the Truths? This constitutes one point of excellence.
If they were not so subsumed, those various inverted views would not be causes of suffering.
Answer: Although the mode of apprehension is inverted, their substance is dependent on others (*paratantra*).
Because there is retribution and there is response, they are subsumed under the Truths of Suffering and Origination.
Within the detailed analysis, this is divided into four sections;
first, the explanation of the Truth of Suffering.
Regarding the statement, "Because of two characteristics, the meaning of impermanence is revealed," Jing says:
First, according to the Mahāyāna, it is explained that the essence of the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (the imagined nature) is eternally non-existent; this is termed "impermanence."
Second, the meaning of the disintegration and destruction of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is termed impermanence (*anitya*).
The Mahāyāna possesses both meanings;
the Hīnayāna possesses only the latter meaning of impermanence.
Xuán says: "The first meaning,
'not being existent,' refers to the impermanence taught in the Mahāyāna,
as explained in the Madhyāntavibhāga-śāstra."
"Having no beginning and being impermanent" refers to the meaning of destruction and disintegration;
this is the impermanence taught by the Hīnayāna.
Regarding the manifestation of suffering through two characteristics:
first, because one thoroughly understands that what is conceptually imputed consists of grasping at a person and phenomena where none exist,
the coarse and heavy latencies [of that grasping] prevent one from attaining mastery over conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*), thereby manifesting the suffering of formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
Second, regarding the meaning of arising accompanied by the three types of sensation and the manifestation of eight kinds of suffering:

the meaning of emptiness and selflessness is that the nature of the afflicted dependent nature—which is the fruit of suffering—is devoid of the fixed characteristics of persons and phenomena as they are imagined by the parikalpita-svabhāva; this is what reveals the meaning of emptiness.
The Mahāyāna elucidates both types of selflessness (*nairātmya*),
whereas the Hīnayāna elucidates only the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*).
Nevertheless, this meaning of emptiness and selflessness—
If one follows the Sarvāstivāda, it speaks only of the emptiness of persons and the selflessness of persons;
if one follows the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, it fully explains both the emptiness of persons and phenomena, as well as the two types of selflessness.
It refers to the teaching on impermanence and the teaching on beginninglessness.
Jingyun: Since manifest results arise from causes, they are impermanent;
it is the nature of things that manifest causes exist prior to their results as something inherently present.
It is called "non-instruction" (avijñapti). Tai says:
that which explains phenomena arising and ceasing moment by moment is called "the teaching on impermanence."
The teaching that explains matters which have been continuously succeeding one another since beginningless time is called the "teaching of no-beginning.

Some commentaries explain that teaching conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) is called the "teaching of impermanence," while teaching unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) is called the "teaching of no-beginning."
Regarding the statement "firstly, by way of inclusion," this means that the mode of impermanence is accompanied by *dausthulya* (coarseness),
or because of the suffering inherent in conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), impermanence is itself suffering.
Regarding the statement "secondly, by way of exclusion, because a self cannot be found within conditioned formations," this is an expression through contraposition.
If one explains the eight types of suffering in accordance with the principle that the nature of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is selfless:
because the five aggregates depend upon one another in a reciprocal manner, they cannot exist independently;
thus, suffering itself is selfless.
Regarding the statement that existence is impermanent but not suffering, this refers to the Truth of the Path and so forth:
because the Path is not a painful feeling, it is not the suffering of pain; because the Path is neither the separation from the beloved nor subject to transformation and decay, it is not suffering.
Nor is it that the object sought is not obtained and thus undergoes transformation and decay.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of transformation and decay:
first, the transformation and decay of pleasant feeling which gives rise to suffering.
Second, the suffering arising from the destruction of what is beloved:
because the path does not arise from the destruction of what is unloved, it is not a suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkha*).
This passage serves as proof that the suffering of dependent origination is termed the suffering of change.
If one follows the *Tattvasiddhi*, the Truth of the Path is impermanent and thus constitutes the Truth of Suffering.
However, if one follows the Sarvāstivāda,
because the arising of the Truth of the Path accords with the intentions of the Noble Ones, it is not suffering.
Regarding the statement that "the origin [of suffering] possesses the four truths and the three cessations," this text serves as proof that suffering and its origin are of the same substance,
because both fully possess the four meanings— suffering and so forth— and the one meaning [of cessation].
That which is said to have the nature of affliction is the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*).
That which is oppressed by suffering is the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
Next, the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*) is explained.
First, regarding the gateway of suffering (*duḥkha*), afflictions and karma are taken as the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*).
Later, it is explained that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is the truth of origination as taught in the Sūtra.
Within the former section, there are two question-and-answer exchanges.
Regarding the beginning and middle [of the Four Noble Truths], according to the Sarvāstivāda, suffering and its origin are two distinct entities consisting of cause and effect.
According to the *Tattvasiddhi* (Satyasiddhi-śāstra), karma and afflictions constitute the Truth of Origin,
while the five aggregates resulting from retribution constitute the Truth of Suffering.
Therefore, suffering and its origin have distinct natures.
Now, according to the Mahāyāna doctrine, there are both similarities and differences.
Regarding the wholesome and indeterminate dharmas within the body of an Arhat:
Although the seeds of the afflictions have been severed, there remain the latencies (*vāsanā*) and the heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*);
therefore, it is also called suffering.
The second question and answer concern the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) categorized as definitive for liberation.

Question: The fifty-first passage cited previously states that according to the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, the "determination of liberation" (*vimukti-viniścaya*) is the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*).
How can this be reconciled with the present statement that it is the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*)?
The answer to Tai states:
"Based on these passages, one knows that,
according to the Mahāyāna doctrine, the three truths are of the same essence."
From the perspective of its capacity to produce desirable results, it is the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*);
from the perspective of being accompanied by coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*), it is the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*);
and from the perspective of its ability to lead forth the untainted Noble Path (*anāsrava-āryamārga*), it is the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*).
Master Sengxuan said:
"The Tripitaka Master did not approve of the previous interpretation and provided a further explanation."
Liberation and its explanation each have two kinds.
First, there are the beginningless, primordially existing seeds of outflows,
which exist within the state of the two [aspects of] words and phenomena.
These are provisionally designated as the two roots of wholesome characteristics.
Second, they are the two types of contaminated wholesome roots subsumed under preparatory knowledge (*prayoga-jñāna*) and subsequent knowledge (*pṛṣṭha-jñāna*).
These are now collectively termed the "Truths."
According to the explanation based on that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*),
it is called the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*) elsewhere;
this is stated in reference to that which is without outflows (*anāsrava*).
Therefore, there is no contradiction.
Below, the sūtra explains that craving is the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*).
In the middle section, first a question is posed and then answered.
In the response, the first part summarizes the four causes and identifies craving (*tṛṣṇā*) as the origin (*samudaya*).
First, because the member of craving grasps [the object], it subsumes all afflictions within itself.
Second, because it assists the member of ignorance (*avidyā*), it sustains all karmic actions.
Regarding the subsequent explanation, we shall next explain each individually; however, we will only explain the latter two.
As for the statement "pervading all things" up to "it is likewise," it is because a single craving results in three types, and thus craving is categorized accordingly.
Because all phenomena are conditioned by [these factors], they are said to pervade all things;
therefore, it is stated that one should know it is likewise so.
"That which is called seeking liberation above" refers to the desire to realize it.
This is because the desire for wholesome dharmas is termed "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*);
yet, this is craving that is not the craving for future existence (*punarbhava-tṛṣṇā*).

Regarding the statement, "or one who possesses [craving] bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) but not bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), namely one born in the form realm": [this refers to such a person].
If, according to the Sarvāstivāda, one born in a higher realm still possesses the craving associated with the desire-realm transformation-mind (nirmāṇacitta) of the four dhyānas,
nevertheless, in the present Mahāyāna system, the desire-realm transformation-mind of the four dhyānas is bound to the four dhyānas themselves and not bound to the desire realm.
Therefore, for one born in the form realm (rūpadhātu), the desire realm is not established, nor are the sensations of the desire realm established.
This statement is made with reference to the two types of maturation regarding present mastery.
However, if considered in terms of the maturation of seeds, there is also the sense of being established.
If that is so, when one dies with the nine types [of minds], how can the body, while situated in a higher realm,
give rise to feelings associated with afflictions of the desire realm?
The explanation is as follows:
It is said that they are "immature" from the perspective of the majority;
alternatively, it may be said that they are immature here because the discussion concerns only maturation through mastery (*vaśitā*).
Therefore, it is said they are immature.
Regarding the statement, "Furthermore, those born in the desire or form realms who have accomplished what was to be done and abide in the supramundane path or the meditative absorption of cessation":
those from the first fruit (srotāpanna) upward are termed "those who have accomplished what was to be done."
When this noble one enters untainted contemplation (*anāsrava-dhyāna*) or enters the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*),
the feelings bound to the desire and form realms do not manifest; because they are not currently active and have already matured,
they do not constitute [a new maturation].

Question: If a noble one (ārya) born in the desire or form realms enters an untainted contemplation (anāsrava-dhyāna) or enters the meditative attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), at that time, there is the manifestation of feeling associated with the ālayavijñāna belonging to the desire or form realms.
How can it be said that both are unripe?
The explanation states:
here, for the time being, this is stated in reference to the experience of the six consciousnesses.
Regarding the statement that one is universally able to initiate fifteen types of meaninglessness:
if one relies on the ten functions according to the Abhidharma-piṭaka of the Hīnayāna,
they correspond to the sixteen [factors] in the *Nyāyānusāra* and as presented therein.
The fifteen marks and characteristics can be understood.
In the sixty-eighth fascicle, the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) is explained next.
There are three kinds of the Truth of Cessation.
That is to say: cessation through deliberation, cessation not through deliberation,
and cessation through impermanence.
The truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*) is comprised solely of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
In this text, first a question and answer are briefly presented;
subsequently, it is explained how the truth of cessation is free from the four faults.

Regarding the statement that the truth of cessation with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirodha-satya*) is attained through the extinction of afflictions (*kleśa*), and the truth of cessation without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa-nirodha-satya*) is attained by depending on that [extinction]:
according to the Sarvāstivāda school, the truth of cessation consists solely in the extinction of the afflictions.
Regarding the essence of the two types of nirvāṇa— with remainder and without remainder—
the Saṃmitīya and Mahāsāṃghika schools are likewise the same as the Sarvāstivāda.
They say:
Untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) abandons the afflictions (*kleśa*);
it does not abandon the retributive fruit (*vipākaphala*). The cessation of this retributive fruit is non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
According to the Sautrāntika masters, however:
By the power of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), future afflictions and suffering do not arise.
The non-arising of these afflictions and suffering is entirely cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Therefore, the extinction of the afflictions is nirvāṇa with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*).
The cessation that is the fruit of power is *nirvāṇa* without remainder.
Although in the Mahāyāna it is later taught that the cessation of afflictions and suffering is called analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*),
the *nirvāṇa* obtained through the severance of afflictions has true suchness (*tathatā*) as its essence.
Therefore, this differs slightly from what is taught in the Sautrāntika school.
Below, it is explained that the Truth of Cessation is free from four faults.
The cessation of extinction and conditioned formations are not necessarily distinct.
To increase the distinctness [of things] is the fault of overestimation (*samāropa*).
Conversely, to cling to their difference and be distracted by it is the opposite of clinging to their unity;
this should be called underestimation (*apavāda*).
Because they grasp cessation and conditioned formations as having the same intrinsic characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*),
it is called the error of conceptualizing them as having an intrinsic characteristic;
thus, the very grasping is itself movement.
"To say it is both different and not different" is the fault of confusion; "to say it is neither" is the fault of contradiction;
and "to say it is both" is the fault of denial, which in older terminology is called the slander of frivolous conceptualization (*prapañca*).
Regarding what is now called the fault of "denial" (apavāda):

because one clings to the notion that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and their cessation are neither different nor non-different, and thus fails to maintain the existence of the dharma-substance, it is termed "denial.
Below follows the explanation of the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*), which consists of three sections.
First, the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is explained; next, the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*);
and finally, the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*).
Within the first [of these], there are three parts.
First, the establishment of the aggregates (*skandha*) for those who are newly matured is based on the fact that for those training in the three trainings, only the eight branches are taught.
Next, the reason for grouping those eight factors of the right path into three aggregates within the sūtras will be explained.
Regarding the statement that "right speech and right action have morality as their root; with morality as their basis, one is able to enjoy all true dharmas":
by taking right speech and right action as the root of morality, one is then able to give rise to meditative concentration.
Through meditative concentration, one attains wisdom and all other virtues.
Furthermore, regarding that which the Blessed One has described as "the nature of the manifestation of a supremely purified mental activity":
This citation is introduced to establish that right speech, action, and livelihood do not have a distinct,
uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) essence of body and speech as asserted in the *Abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*; rather,
they consist simply of the mental intention (*cetanā*) manifesting in a way that is free from wrong speech and so forth.
Therefore, it is said that "pure mental activity manifests," and so forth.
Regarding the statement that "one relies on greed and so forth to give rise to the volition of violating precepts":
according to the *Abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*, bodily and vocal actions arising from hatred and delusion are termed "wrong speech" (*mithyāvāk-karman*).
If one engages in bodily or vocal actions based on greed, it is called wrong livelihood. Now,
speaking according to the Mahāyāna,
if one engages in the volition of violating the precepts based on greed, hatred, or delusion, it is called wrong speech and action.
If one relies on hypocrisy and the like to give rise to thoughts of seeking food, clothing, and so forth in a wrong manner, this is called wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*).
It should be understood that if one is free from the three aforementioned wrongs,
this constitutes the nature of the manifestation of right speech, right action, and right livelihood.
To say that "thoroughly penetrating the true meaning of all phenomena" is the first activity refers to the activity of right view;
to "proclaiming [the Dharma] to others" and so forth is the second activity.
This refers to the karma of right reflection (*samyak-saṃkalpa*).
This is spoken according to the teachings based on the discursive mind;
however, if one is in a contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) meditative concentration (*samādhi*), this karma does not exist.

"Practicing in accordance with the Dharma for the sake of severing the remaining fetters is the third activity" means that initiating diligent effort in order to sever those remaining [defilements] to be abandoned through cultivation is the activity of diligence.
Question: Right thought (samyak-saṃkalpa) consists of vitarka and is a conventional dharma;
it takes wisdom (prajñā) and mental volition (manas-karma) as its essence.
How does it differ from right view (samyak-dṛṣṭi)?
The commentary states:
Right thought and right view are established solely within the category of object-specific mental factors (*viṣayapratiniyatadharma*);
that is, they consist of a single wisdom (*prajñā*) that serves as the antidote to wrong view and wrong thought.
The [eightfold] path is established based on two factors.
Furthermore, right view may be established in relation to wisdom (*prajñā*), and right thought (*samyaksaṃkalpa*) may be established in relation to volition (*cetanā*).
Since their bases differ, those that depend upon them also differ.
Question: If right thought (*samyak-saṃkalpa*) is established based on volition (*cetanā*),
and right speech, action, and livelihood are also established based on volition,
how can four paths (*mārgāṅga*) be established within a single moment of volition?
The commentary states:
What fault would there be in establishing the four branches of the Noble Eightfold Path by way of abandoning the four branches of the wrong path through the manifestation of mental volition?
Regarding the statement that one binds and collects the mind within the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*):
in the older sūtras and śāstras, the four foundations of mindfulness were held to have wisdom (*prajñā*) alone as their essential nature;
at present, however, they are understood to have both mindfulness (*smṛti*) and wisdom as their essential nature.
In this passage, the essence of mindfulness (*smṛti*) is specifically described as the basis for concentration (*samādhi*).
Regarding the statement that one "individually reaches the point where one can sever all hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*)," the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*),
which grasps at purity, is treated by means of the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).
The hindrance of ill-will has hostility and harm as its nature;
its antidote is the contemplation of loving-kindness and compassion, and so forth.
Below, it is explained that there are eleven types of distinctions in right view.
Within this, first, the eleven right views are correlated with the four truths;
second, the sequence from the sūtra is presented as questions and answers;
third, the eleven right views are shown to encompass the three gates of liberation.
Among these, the first eight views are right views that take the truth of suffering as their object.
The latter three views take, in their respective order, the truths of origination, cessation, and the path as their objects.
As for what are called the view of emptiness and the view of non-self:
To contemplate the aggregates as being devoid of self and what belongs to self is called the view of emptiness.
To contemplate the essential nature of those conditioned phenomena as lacking the characteristics of self and what belongs to self is called the view of non-self.
This differs from the Sarvāstivāda explanation, which holds that contemplating the emptiness of "mine" is called the practice of emptiness,
while contemplating the emptiness of the "self" is called the practice of non-self.
Next, the sequence from the sūtra is cited to provide the questions and answers.
Question: The *Itivuttaka* explains the sequence by first teaching the four views beginning with impermanence (*anicca*), and subsequently teaching the views beginning with "like a disease" (*roga*).
For what reason, then, does this [text] first teach "like a disease" and so forth?
The answer consists of two successive stages:
first, the sequence of entering the state of a noble one prior to the path of vision (*darśanamārga*),
which involves first contemplating such practices as impermanence (*anityatā*).
Subsequently, one contemplates the contaminated [phenomena] as being like a disease and like an abscess.
Later, upon emerging from the path of seeing, within the path of cultivation, one first contemplates them through such modes as being like a disease;
subsequently, for the sake of extinguishing the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation, one gives rise to modes of contemplation such as impermanence.
The following clarifies the meaning of the preceding section.
Briefly stated, there are two kinds:
first, those based on views such as viewing [the body] as like a disease, which are impure views and so forth.
That is to say, during the stage of an ordinary person prior to this path of seeing, performing such mental applications as [contemplating] impermanence and so forth can lead one toward it;
this is called the "impurity-based pure vision" that serves as the basis.
Second, regarding "the pure vision and so forth that depend on the vision of [phenomena] as being like a disease, etc.":
having already emerged from the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*),
one again gives rise to the vision of [phenomena] as being like a disease, etc., during the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
It is pure because it arises within the noble body (*āryakāya*).
Such a vision arises by the power of causes—such as the vision of [all things] as being like a disease and so forth—prior to the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).
Since this is that which depends [upon the path], the path is the support, and thus it is the purity of the support.
Furthermore, within the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), the practices such as impermanence (*anityatā*) can be described as the basis (*āśraya*),
just as the practices such as being like a disease (*roga*) serve as that which is based upon it (*āśrita*).
Below, eleven forms of right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) are cited to subsume the three gates of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*).

The views of emptiness and selflessness are called the practice of emptiness (*śūnyatā-carita*), because they share the same objective support (*ālambana*) of the absence of self and what belongs to a self (*anātman-anātmiya*).
The other views are called the practice of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-carita*); these eight views are referred to as "the others."
The first type of view is called the "practice of signlessness" (*animitta-caryā*).
This refers to the eleventh [view], because it takes the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*) as its object.
This is the same as in the *Hṛdaya-śāstra* (Small Treatise).
Two aspects are emptiness;
ten aspects are wishlessness;
four aspects are signlessness.
However, these three gates differ from the eight textual passages regarding their inclusion within the aspects of practice (*ākāra*),
as recorded in the twelfth fascicle of the *Maulī Bhūmi* mentioned previously.
Second, in explaining the cultivation of the path (*bhāvanāmārga*), there are two successive expositions.
Next, regarding the middle section:
within the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), one takes the four noble truths as objects;
this serves as the skillful means for entering the contemplation of suchness (*tathatā-darśana*) and severing the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation.
Regarding the statement "those who have seen the tracks" up to "having reached clear observation": this refers to the path of seeing characterized by signs.

Conventional knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*) is called "manifest" because it takes what is below as its object; subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) is called "non-manifest" because it takes what is above as its object.
The Tripitaka Master, following the *Abhidharmakośa*, explains this passage as follows:
"In the category of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*), the realization of suchness is termed 'manifest';
in the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), the realization of the category of dharma-knowledge is termed 'unmanifest'."
Having attained the first fruit,
one contemplates the suffering of the three realms and the origin of the three realms in their entirety;
this continues until the path of the three realms in its entirety serves as the remote preparatory application (*dūre-prayoga*).
Next, one further contemplates the Four Truths of the three realms as empty and selfless.
From this, one immediately realizes the *tathatā* (suchness) manifested through the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
One then completely severs the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation across the nine stages.
Having transcended to the realization of arhatship,

this differs from the dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) of the Abhidharma, which takes the suchness (*tathatā*) as its object, whereas the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) takes the preceding dharma-knowledge as its object.

As for the statement that "the subsequent [knowledge], in the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), is able to generally counteract all afflictions (*kleśa*) of the lower and higher stages," it refers to this.
This passage explains that one may skip the realization of arhatship by completely abandoning the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) from the very first fruit.
Tai states:
"This is based on treating the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation across the nine stages (*navabhūmi*) of the three realms as a single set of nine grades."
Furthermore, one takes all defiled phenomena within the three realms collectively as suffering and its origin;
one takes all undefiled categories of phenomena within the three realms collectively as cessation and the path.
By contemplating the Four Truths of the three realms as a whole, one employs this as the skillful means for entering the signless contemplation (*animitta-vipaśyanā*).
Therefore, the afflictions of the nine stages are collectively categorized into nine grades,
which are abandoned through nine paths of uninterrupted activity and nine paths of liberation.
Among them, there are noble ones who abandon the afflictions of the nine stages across the three realms individually.
They are distinct dharmas and types;
Xuán provides two explanations.
One says:

This text is based on the argument that a Bodhisattva, by means of the single unimpeded path of the vajra-like samādhi, suddenly severs the nine grades of afflictions to be abandoned through the path of cultivation within the three realms.
One source states:
"This is based on the argument concerning the transcendence of arhatship."
Next, it says:
"Furthermore, those noble ones, up to the point of having severed the afflictions," refers to the mental application of signlessness (*animitta-manasikāra*),
which is non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
Regarding the application of attention (*manasikāra*) during the stage of cultivation, many practitioners engage in this contemplation.
Third, the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*) is clarified;
therein, the mention of the "five supernormal powers" (*pañcābhijñā*) and so forth refers to these.
Regarding the intention to take up the sages:
although the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) are with-outflow (*sāsrava*), because they are attained subsequent to the outflow-free state,
their nature is pure and is subsumed under the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).
As stated above, the categories of the path of accumulation (*sambhāramārga*) and the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*) are all subsumed under the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).
The five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*) of non-Buddhist outsiders do not enter these categories;
they are not subsumed under the Truth of the Path.
From here below is the third section, the analysis of various categories.
Within this, there are six sections;
the first clarifies the establishment and abolition of the names of the truths as eternally severed by omniscience.
Regarding the statement that the Truth of Suffering is specifically termed "thoroughly known" (*parijñāta*):
it is because it is to be thoroughly known through two types of application.
Knowledge of the practice of suffering is the thorough knowledge of its specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
One contemplates suffering through the practice of impermanence;
this is the universal thorough knowledge of the three truths.
One knows suffering through the practices of emptiness and non-self.
One thoroughly knows suffering through the practice of all phenomena;
therefore, it is called the common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).
