For example, if one refuses food due to being afflicted by illness, or if one stands while urinating or defecating, these are also called non-offenses and are termed "emergencies.
Seventh, regarding emergence due to obstacles and difficulties: this refers to encountering life-threatening danger.
The seven transgressions regarding trees are permitted without offense;
these are termed "renunciation" (*niḥsaraṇa*) and so forth.
These two types of renunciation will be explained below in the text.
8. Because of the white [robes], for the sake of the Buddha;
9. Having made the announcement, one assembles the community, because the Buddha’s establishment of the precepts must take place within the community;
10. Because once the monastic community has assembled, there is first the prohibition and subsequently the allowance.
This is because it enables one to attain ultimate freedom from affliction and harm.
Third, the discernment of renunciation:
therein, "renunciation free from defilement" is mentioned.
If one has a virtuous mind when pulling weeds or grass before a Buddha, this is permitted within the Mahāyāna.
If one increases one's own goodness and diminishes evil, there is no transgression;
this is precisely what is called renunciation.
Regarding the term "minor concomitants" (anuvartaka), it is as explained in the commentary of the preceding fascicle.
As for the phrase "lacking the calculation of deliverance," Jing says:
In the midst of wildernesses, where there are dangers such as insects and wolves,
it is permitted to carry knives and hold staves for self-defense.
Tai says:
Since it is impossible to enjoy things in dangerous places according to the Dharma,
one should develop reverence for the teachings and fear toward transgressions,
having no other recourse.
To intentionally perform such an act without committing an offense is called "having no calculation for deliverance.
Xuán says:
If there is no one available to receive it, one may consume it oneself without offense.
Fourth, regarding the cessation [of the rule]:
the mention therein is intended to prevent those who would otherwise find it difficult to survive.
As stated in the Vinaya, during times of scarcity eight exceptions were permitted:
namely, "storing within" (antarāvasatha) and "cooking within" (antarasamāpanna).
Cooking for oneself;
taking food with one's own hands;
accepting morning meals.
Carrying remnants from the place of eating,
such as rice, walnuts, fruits, and so forth;
or edible items found within drinking water— examples such as these.
Fifth, regarding the statement "ten types of *karmas*" within the *Karmavācanā*:
first, performing the *karma* at the time of receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*);
second, establishing the great and small boundaries (*sīmā*).
The Elder Jingyun said:
"It is like the young son of a high minister or perhaps a prince who wishes to leave the household life;
there would be great benefit in his doing so within the Buddha-dharma."
However, they were unable to abstain from eating at improper times; thus,
the great assembly prepared gruel to nourish their minds and performed the *karmavācanā* to authorize the mixing of various medicinal substances.
"Prepare congee for them, ensuring that the grains do not show.
Tai said:
"Posadha-karman is translated here as 'nurturing' (changyang)."
This nourishes and develops merit.
Regarding the fourth, "agreement in intention," Jingyun said:
it is like one who has attained the first fruit [of the path], who feels no attachment or stinginess toward clothing or food.
The bhikṣus vied with one another to go begging for alms, which ultimately led to poverty and suffering.
At that time, the great assembly reached a consensus and collectively performed a *karmavācanā* (formal ecclesiastical act) to resolve the matter. Tái said:
The *karmavācanā* for the formal act (*karman*) is that which harmonizes the Sangha so that their intentions are one.
Regarding the "five approaches," Jing says:
it is as when a nun wishes to approach the great assembly of monks to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*).
First, one performs the formal ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*) among the community of nuns;
subsequently proceeding to the location of the great assembly of monks (*bhikṣu-saṃgha*) is called "the ritual procedure of proceeding" (*abhisamācārika-karman*).
T'ai states that this refers to performing the ritual procedure for entering the place of summer retreat (*varṣā*).
Sixth, *pravāraṇā-udghāta* refers to the formal raising of charges at the end of the summer retreat (*varṣā*).
Seventh, *daṇḍakarma* (punishment) refers to the disciplinary measures for those who have committed offenses, such as the seven types of *karmavācanā*.
Eighth, *saṃgraha* (reception) refers to the community first disciplining wicked individuals and causing them to leave the assembly.
Having been disciplined for some time, he repented of his former deeds;
the assembly performed the *karmavācanā* to admit him back into the community, which is termed "acceptance" (*parigraha*).
The first eight [cases] concern specific matters, while the final two clarify the formal procedures (*dharma*).
Regarding the five types of *pudgala*:
first is the "analogy of excellent wisdom," who judges the text based on its meaning.
Second, the parable of the two parrots,
which determines the meaning based on the text;
third, the parable of the person with a torch.
This refers to one who has heard little but possesses great understanding,
like a lamp or candle that is passed along from one to another.
Fourth is the person likened to a flash of lightning.
Regarding the ten types of *karmavācanā* previously mentioned,
they are sometimes momentarily resolved and sometimes not perceived,
like a flash of lightning.
The fifth is the analogy of calligraphy and painting,
which represents people who follow the text in their actions,
neither adding to nor subtracting from it.
The preceding section has distinguished the authentic;
from here on, the spurious shall be distinguished.
To say that something does not enter into the sūtras means it does not accord with the sūtras (sūtra).
That which does not appear in the Vinaya is non-conformable to the Vinaya;
that which contradicts the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is contrary to the Abhidharma.
This is the twelfth explanation.
Regarding the statement in the middle section, "excluding ten kinds of matters... one should know that this is not a pure teaching":
if, as stated below, one speaks to another person about the ten kinds of matters such as the corruption of precepts or views, [it is not a pure teaching].
However, this refers to a pure exposition that excludes ten matters.
If a bhikṣu, in the presence of another person, speaks of another bhikṣu’s violation of precepts, views, or other such faults, it is not a pure exposition.
Regarding the ten matters that should be confessed to others:
first, the intent to harm the Buddha;
second, [the intent to harm] the Dharma.
Third, regarding the Saṃgha:
because it causes harm to the Three Jewels, one may even speak to the king about it;
however, this is considered a pure speech.
Regarding the phrase "the four views, by means of those [views], destroy precepts and views":
it causes other bhikṣus to further break their precepts, views, and so forth;
thus, that evil assembly gradually decays and increases, whether through hearing or through doubt.
One speaks to others to cause the evil assembly to cease.
Fifth, one sees that they themselves manifest the destruction of their precepts, views, conduct, livelihood, and other such unrighteous dharmas;
this one either hears of or suspects.
Sixth, wishing to cause them to emerge from [wrong] views and the destruction of precepts,
and to establish them in wholesome states,
he speaks to others. Seventh, all the bhikṣus have likewise destroyed their precepts, views, and so forth.
For the sake of protecting other laypeople,
they further conceal one another's faults, causing all manner of evils to increase daily;
therefore, one must also speak to others [of these faults] so that the evils may cease.
Eighth, there may be a donor, or even the founder of a monastery and others, who address the Saṃgha, saying:
"If any bhikṣus residing here are seen to have violated their precepts or hold wrong views, you should inform me."
If the entire community of monks hears these words together,
they must also speak them to the donor and others;
this too is a pure proclamation.
Ninth, if one sees that because of causes and conditions such as the corruption of the monastic community’s precepts and views,
kings and others harbor resentment within their hearts and wish to initiate harmful and disadvantageous actions.
Whether one has heard it or suspects it,
one must also speak of it to others;
this is called "pure speech."

When a group of ten monks has corrupted their families and engaged in evil conduct through the destruction of precepts and views, there is no power or ability to discipline them except for one single means: speaking to others; this is what is meant by "pure speech."

Regarding the phrase "defiling a family and practicing evil conduct," it is as explained in the Vinaya under the precept concerning the expulsion and censure of those who defile families and refuse to heed admonition.
Regarding the phrase "if due to jealousy and so forth," [it refers to the following].
To speak with the intent to disparage by means of the ten aforementioned causes and conditions, such as jealousy and so forth,
is called impure speech.
This is the thirteenth explanation of the illustrative matter.
Regarding the mention of "birth stories" (jātaka),
this refers to speaking of the deeds performed by the Bodhisattva in previous lives as metaphors.
Regarding "original life stories" (itivṛttaka):
This means that the various external, corresponding matters of the Bodhisattva’s bodies in previous lives are taught as metaphors.
As for the matter of the reflected image,
it refers to teaching the sequence from milk and curd up to clarified butter (*sarpis*) as metaphors for the Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*).
The "similarity of images" refers to citing those who are preeminent among persons.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the seven kinds of rivers in the world," this refers to the seven types of sentient beings within the river of birth and death mentioned in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
The subsequent explanation of the seven persons within the river of nirvāṇa reveals the seven types of persons within the True Dharma.
The first is "constantly submerged."
Second, having briefly emerged, he sinks back down.
Third, having reached the surface, he remains stationary.
Fourth, having emerged, he gazes all around in the four directions.
Fifth, having observed them all around, he proceeds;
sixth, having proceeded, he returns and stands still;
seventh, he travels both on water and on land.
The detailed explanation is as in that [text].
Regarding the "conventionally compounded matter," this refers to the analogy of the great king or the analogy of the skilled physician.
Jing says:
As the World-Honored One has said, the sixth king is the most excellent.
As it is said that an Arhat eliminates the disease of the afflictions,
just as a skilled physician can eliminate all poisons.
Tài says:
"Sometimes the Great King, sometimes the skilled physician, and so forth—through the conjunction of many such things, these serve as metaphors for the Buddha and others.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that there are worldly similes perceived through direct experience that correspond at least to a small degree," [it means:]
As it is said: do the seeds of affliction and the untainted seeds rely upon the same basis?
They are like filth and pure gold existing in the same place.
Regarding "illustrative matters," this refers to extensive, lengthy, and numerous similes and so forth.
As it is said, when a single parable is explained through immeasurable causes and conditions,
it is called a "long parable" (dīrgha-avadāna),
such as the Parable of the Burning House and others.
Of the three sections into which the definitive analysis (*viniścaya*) of this stage has been divided above, the first two have now been concluded.
Below, the third section provides an extensive and miscellaneous definitive analysis by means of sixty-four gates.
First, the phenomena that are objects of knowledge (*jñeya-dharma*) are explained.
Within this, first the distinctions of the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) are established by means of five aspects,
followed by an analysis of the distinctions among the various types of knowledge (*jñāna*).
Regarding the former, the five aspects are listed in sequence and then explained.
Regarding the statement that "if one can, according to worldly convention, know the designated objects of knowledge, up to those portions that should be cultivated," the question is:
how does one understand the designation of phenomena such as the wholesome and unwholesome, the blameworthy and blameless, and dependent origination as being "designated knowledge"?
The commentary states:
These various phenomena, if considered in relation to objects such as jars or basins, should be called substantial dharmas (*dravyadharma*);
however, when considered in relation to the principles of the Truths (*satya*) such as suffering, they are termed ultimate (*paramārtha*).
Therefore, it is said that the arising of offenses, merits, and so forth through conditions is termed "provisionally established.
One portion, such as the unwholesome, should be abandoned; another portion, such as the wholesome, should be cultivated.
Furthermore, regarding the statement "one can also fully understand up until the point where one initiates various practices":
Knowing that conventional discourse gives rise to designations for worldly phenomena is called "wandering in the world.

To initiate various activities in accordance with these names and expressions is the gateway of reasoning concerning the turning [of the wheel] according to the dispositions and latent tendencies of others.
They are planted within the six consciousnesses;
the mental inclination is the desire,
and the latent tendency is the seed.
Because one knows the minds of others through their six consciousnesses,
the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) that follow and accompany those minds are also said to be known. Furthermore,
this may also refer to the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) attained from the first bhūmi upward.
To know the *ālaya*-consciousness and its seeds—
stating that there are two types of bases for knowledge, namely (1) practice for one's own benefit and (2) practice for the benefit of others—
refers precisely to the five aforementioned wisdoms of activity.
The first three types [of knowledge] are free from doubt regarding their objects;
they are called the bases for practice based on one's own benefit.
The latter two know the matters such as the faculties, karma, and so forth of those to be converted.
It is named "relying on the practice of benefiting others" as its basis.

As for the statement that conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) pervades the three natures, pervades both the outflowing (*sāsrava*) and the non-outflowing (*anāsrava*), and is exclusively mundane (*laukika*):
this corresponds to the knowledge of the *Abhidharma* and so forth.

Regarding the statement that conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) pertains to all three natures and is exclusively contaminated (sāsrava), whereas this [knowledge] pertains to both the contaminated and the uncontaminated (anāsrava):
it is called "uncontaminated" because it arises within the body of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) who is free from outflows.
Regarding the statement that this and the remainder are collectively termed "conventional knowledge" (saṃvṛtijñāna):

it means that the impure wisdom of the three natures present within the body of one beyond training (aśaikṣa), as well as that present within the bodies of ordinary persons (pṛthagjana) and those in training (śaikṣa), are all collectively designated as conventional knowledge.
It should be understood that the remaining dharmas— namely, the knowledge of categories (*anvaya-jñāna*), the knowledge of suffering, origination, cessation, and the path,

as well as the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*)— arise solely within the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*). Because they are exclusively supramundane, they are exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*),
being in accordance with the wisdom of reality (*yathābhūta-jñāna*).
Regarding the statement, "If one makes such a distinction, it is subsumed under conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) and so forth," this refers to subsequent knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
Because it employs the term "distinction," it is called mundane;
yet, because it has never been attained before and arises within the body of an Arhat, it is also called supramundane (*lokottara*).
Regarding the statement that "the knowledge of others' minds is exclusively mundane," a question is raised:
since the knowledge of others' minds possessed by those in training (*śaikṣa*) is indeed contaminated (*sāsrava*),
how can it know uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) minds?
The commentary explains:
Although they belong to the same class of practitioners,
one uses a tainted mind-knowledge (*sāsrava-paracitta-jñāna*) to know another’s untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*).
What fault would there be in this?
For instance, when the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) belonging to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) knows a mind of the form realm,

it does not— as the Lesser Treatises (*Hīnayāna-śāstra*) maintain— that the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) knowledge of others' minds knows only the tainted minds of others and cannot know untainted (*anāsrava*) minds.
One does not know the mind and so forth of the formless realm.
Regarding the statement that "the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising should be understood as before," this refers to when they are not distinguished as supramundane.

If one discriminates that both the mundane and the untainted (*anāsrava*) are equal, this is the "knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows" (*āsravakṣaya-jñāna*), which pervades both the mundane and the supramundane; it is exclusively untainted and is comprised within the gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*) and the eight knowledges (*aṣṭajñāna*). Thus it is said.
Excluding conventional knowledge and the knowledge of others' minds,
when this wisdom of the gate of emptiness seeks to enter the contemplation of *tathatā* (suchness),
it first contemplates the meaning of the emptiness and selflessness of all phenomena.
When the eight knowledges are contemplated as such,
the emptiness and selflessness of the Four Truths correspond in meaning to the contemplation of the four knowledges of suffering and so forth;
the emptiness of the lower desire realm corresponds in meaning to the contemplation of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*).
The meaning of emptiness regarding the two upper realms corresponds to this wisdom.
When present within the body of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), it constitutes the two knowledges of exhaustion (*kṣaya*) and non-arising (*anutpāda*).
Thus, it is known that the number of meditative concentrations associated with these eight knowledges constitutes the liberation door of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*).
The following section distinguishes the varieties of knowledge (*jñāna*).
Within this, there are seven parts.
The first presents the gates of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*), the unique qualities (*āveṇikadharma*), the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), and so forth.
This refers to what was previously explained.
First, the elucidation of the various supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā-jñāna*),
which is divided into three parts.
First, the names and meanings of the six supernormal knowledges (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) are clarified;
next, the persons who possess these supernormal powers are clarified;
finally, they are collectively clarified through comparative analysis.
Regarding the beginning: "What is the supernormal power (ṛddhi)? asks about that which is transformed.
"What is the knowledge of supernormal power (ṛddhividhi-jñāna)? asks about that which performs the transformation.
"What is the realization through the knowledge of supernormal power (ṛddhividhi-jñānasākṣātkriyā)? asks about the act of realization.
Question: What are the causes and conditions for cultivating and realizing the supernormal knowledge of the power of transformation (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna*),
specifically that which involves transforming one form into many through luminous transformation,
and even exercising mastery over the body as far as the Brahma-world?
It is explained that this is called "supernormal power" (*ṛddhi*) because it is that which is operated by the knowledge of supernormal power (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna*);
this is the etymological explanation of the term "supernormal power."
This answers the first question.
The statement "if it is knowledge" up to "is therefore called the knowledge of supernormal power" answers the second question.
It is designated as the fruit of cultivation because it distinguishes this from knowledge acquired through birth and so forth.

Regarding the statement, "This very seed of wisdom, up to what is called the realization through the knowledge of supernormal powers (ṛddhividhi-jñāna-sākṣātkriyā)," the answer is that it refers to the third realization.
Question: Since all sentient beings have possessed the seeds of supernormal powers since beginningless time and have repeatedly attained them, do they not all possess these seeds?
Because of the presence of the obstacles of existence and the obstacles of phenomena, one is unable to give rise to supernormal powers.
Now, at this time, the practitioner, by virtue of having abandoned these two obstacles,
causes the old seeds to increase and continue through the power of cultivation.
At that time, because the conditions are complete, the supernormal powers (abhijñā) can arise;
thus it is said: "These very seeds are sustained by generative conditions," and so forth. All of this is subsumed under one name:

the supernormal power of the realization of the knowledge of the base of psychic power (*ṛddhiviṣayajñānasākṣātkriyābhijñā*). This refers to the knowledge of the base of psychic power and the realization combined, which is collectively termed the supernormal power of the realization of the knowledge of the base of psychic power.
The statement "it is said that the various minds of others [are known] by means of having greed and so forth" clarifies the objective range of the supernormal power of knowing others' minds;
it refers to the ten pairs of minds, such as those with greed and those without greed.
The phrase "if one possesses great majestic power (*mahānubhāva*) and so forth" clarifies the essence of the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
Regarding the statement "it should be understood that this wisdom realizes [its object] as previously described," this means that these seeds,
being sustained by the conditions for their arising, increase and develop within the continuum.

Regarding the statement, "If one takes as a basis the pure matter subsumed under the eye that has been cultivated as a result," the supernormal power of the divine eye (divya-cakṣus) has as its essence the wisdom associated with visual consciousness.
However, when other texts state that [the knowledge] takes the future and so forth as its object,
this is discussed in reference to the entire retinue associated with the mental consciousness. Furthermore,
the "knowledge of the destruction of outflows" (*āsravakṣaya-jñāna*) is designated as the "knowledge of exhaustion" (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the "knowledge of non-arising" (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
According to the Sarvāstivāda school, there are two senses:
first, they are designated as six types of knowledge based on their objects of cognition;
second, they are established as distinct entities within the person.
These ten knowledges (*jñāna*) are by nature both outflowing (*sāsrava*) and non-outflowing (*anāsrava*).
Now, in the Mahāyāna, they take as their essence only the mundane knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the mundane knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
Next, regarding those who possess the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), Jing says:
If one is able to manifest [powers] upon encountering the appropriate occasion, this is the supernormal power of the base of psychic transformation (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna*).
Alternatively, "abiding" refers to hearing sounds with the divine ear (*divya-śrotra*),
and knowing the distinctions in the mental activities of others through the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*).
However, while one may understand what is to be known and abide in peace for oneself, one has not yet been able to extensively engage in activities that lead others [to the same].
To say that one either acts for the benefit of others through speech or conduct, or is capable of skillfully answering questions regarding these matters, refers to the latter three [stages].
Through the knowledge of past lives, he knows the various births others have previously undergone;
with the divine eye, he sees beings dying here and being born there;
and through the destruction of the outflows, he realizes the unconditioned.
Thus, being aware of the three times, he knows the past, future, and present events of others and preaches the Dharma according to their capacities;
therefore, it is said that he "is able to skillfully answer questions. Tai says:
Alternatively, those who abide [in peace] manifest for their own sport,
while those who act for the benefit of others manifest for the sake of benefiting them.
The following section generally clarifies the distinctions between the paths, without discussing the specific modes of manifestation.
Regarding the statement that the latter three [knowledges] enable one to sever views of permanence and annihilation from afar:
through the knowledge of past lives, one knows the causal conditions of others' pasts and teaches them so as to cause them to abandon the view of permanence.
With the divine eye, he knows that others will undergo birth and death in the future;
he shows them the way to lead them away from the view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*).
As for the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*), he proclaims the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*).
Regarding the three types of clear knowledge (*vidyā*), the absence of conflict (*araṇā*), and the knowledge resulting from resolve (*praṇidhijñāna*):
the text is divided into three parts.
First, the absence of conflict is explained; next, the knowledge resulting from resolve is explained.
The subsequent section clarifies that the Buddha does not enter the concentration of non-contention (araṇā-samādhi) frequently.
This section consists of three parts;
the first clarifies the cultivation of the concentration of non-contention through three types of causes and conditions.
Next, the name "Araṇā" (Non-contention) is explained;
subsequently, the protection exercised during the practice of Non-contention is clarified.
First, it is stated that an Arhat of sharp faculties who is liberated both ways dwells in Non-contention.
The Abhidharma merely states that those of sharp faculties who are immovable attain it,
but does not mention those liberated in both ways; here, however, we speak of those liberated in both ways,
for one must first attain the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) before cultivating the absence of conflict (*araṇā*).
The section beginning with "Regarding what has arisen within oneself" explains the definition.
The section beginning with "In this manner" clarifies the protection to be maintained during cultivation.
Next, it clarifies that the knowledge resulting from vows must first involve the formulation of a vow.
Having entered the meditative absorption of the ultimate limit (prāntakoṭika-samādhi) and completed its cultivation,
one then knows that the vow-knowledge (praṇidhijñāna) of each of the three vehicles penetrates and realizes its respective sphere of objects as known.
The following clarifies that the Buddha does not frequently enter the concentration of non-contention (*araṇā-samādhi*).
This means that if there are those who should be tamed through the arousal of contention, he engages in debate with them; therefore, he does not enter it repeatedly.
The fourth point clarifies the distinctions among the various types of knowledge induced by relying on meditative concentration.
Just as the fourth dhyāna serves as the basis for inducing the knowledge of non-contention (*araṇā*) and the knowledge resulting from prayer (*praṇidhijñāna*),
one should know that the sublime wisdom of the Tathāgata’s unique qualities (*āveṇikadharma*) is likewise.
Based on this textual evidence, it is proven that all the virtues of the Tathāgata depend upon the fourth dhyāna.
Furthermore, by this same proof, it is established that the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) likewise depend upon all four dhyānas,
differing from the assertions of the Hinayana treatises.
The five types of clear knowledge (*pañca-vidyā*) rely exclusively on the first five stages (*bhūmi*) for their initial entry into the state of a noble one (*ārya*).
This is because prior to the preparatory concentrations (*sāmantaka*), the fundamental concentrations (*mauladhyāna*) do not yet exist.
Those noble ones enter the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) by relying upon the "not-yet-reached" concentration (*anāgamya*).
Because the first fundamental dhyāna already exists prior to the preparatory concentration (*anāgamya*) of the second dhyāna and is capable of producing the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) state,
the preparatory stages (*prayoga*) of the seven higher stages do not produce the outflow-free state unless they are the *anāgamya*.
Sixth, the distinction between the three temporal limits of mundane and supramundane wisdom.
First, the general introduction is presented, followed by the formal analysis.
Within the formal analysis, there are two parts.
First, mundane wisdom is explained, followed by supramundane wisdom.
Within mundane wisdom, first the mundane wisdom of the two vehicles regarding the three periods of time is explained,
and subsequently the mundane wisdom of Bodhisattvas regarding the three periods of time is explained.
In the preceding section, the conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) that first arises at the initial limit was clarified;
it is said to be for the purpose of giving rise to its antidote.
Subsequently, there arises the innate knowledge (*upapattipratilambhika-jñāna*) which is non-erroneous and embraced by worldly faith.
Taking this as the sequence for the arising of hearing, reflection, and so forth, these are the five contemplations (*pañca-sthāpanā*).

Taking this as the sequence for that which is subsumed under the contaminated conventional knowledge (*sāsrava-saṃvṛti-jñāna*) within the path of skillful means conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya-prayoga-mārga*), these are the general and specific applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).

Taking these as the sequential means for the arising of the path of seeing, the "wisdom of decisive discernment" and so forth refer to the three roots of goodness, namely *ūṣmagata*, *mūrdhan*, and *kṣānti*.
Furthermore, immediately following this, the conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) of the intermediate period is explained.
The statement that "at the time of ascending to the path of vision (darśanamārga), it is also called cultivation" is intended to distinguish it from the five defiled views (*dṛṣṭi*) and so forth.
The statement that "it is the wholesome conventional knowledge (*sāṃvṛtijñāna*)" is because it arises through the power of the non-defiled perfuming (*vāsanā*) of the path of vision.
It causes the seeds of the three types of mundane wisdom (*sāsrava-prajñā*) to increase and become purified.
Having emerged from the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one gives rise to this wisdom to realize liberation from all phenomena to be abandoned through seeing.
Having emerged from the path of seeing, one gives rise to this knowledge and speaks thus:
"I have forever severed the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing;
I have forever exhausted all evil destinies."
It is called the liberation through the realization and vision of all phenomena to be abandoned.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "one should establish for others whatever is to be declared according to their needs," it is by means of this wisdom that one establishes the teaching for others.
Furthermore, by means of this wisdom, one is able to discern pure and impure phenomena and provide explanations for others;
one is also able to establish instruction for others regarding the direct realization (*abhisamaya*) of the noble truths (*āryasatya*).
As for the statement that "furthermore, from this point upward, one may even depart from those desires by means of the mundane path (*laukikamārga*)," it refers to this.
The *Bùquè* (Supplement) states:

This passage explains that the noble ones are the same as ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) insofar as they use the sixfold worldly wisdom (*laukikajñāna*) to suppress the afflictions of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) and subsequently abandon them through cultivation.
Tai said:
According to this text,
it appears that even those at the stage of the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) are able to abandon desire by means of the mundane path (*laukikamārga*).
However, there would be the fault that a stream-enterer could be reborn in a higher realm,
as well as the fault that they could enter the meditative attainment of cessation;
therefore, this cannot be established as definitive.
One must further examine other sūtras and śāstras.
There is a separate *Dharmacakrapravartana-sūtra*,
which states that those who have attained the first fruit are also reborn in the higher realms.

A certain master explains that this passage provides a general explanation of how conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) can suppress the afflictions (*kleśa*) and attain meditative concentration (*samādhi*),
at which time one attains the first fruit (*prathamaphala*).
Therefore, it is said that above this, according to what is appropriate,
one should not say that the fruit of the first stage (*prathamaphala*) enters meditative concentration by suppressing the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Guo says:
A stream-enterer suppresses and abandons the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) and attains the first dhyāna;
this continues up to suppressing the afflictions of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) and attaining the perception-sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).
The intermediate and final limits are to be understood according to the text.
The following clarifies the bodhisattva’s wisdom regarding the three periods of time.
Regarding the statement, "Furthermore, among the various stages (bhūmi), bodhisattvas initiate two kinds of practices," etc.,
the *Bǔquè* (Supplement) states:

Subsequent knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), which observes the capacities of beings and establishes teachings and so forth, is called "practice involving the manifestation of conceptual proliferation regarding signs" (*prapañca-saṃjñā-vikalpa-pravṛtti*).
Non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) is called "practice free from the manifestation of conceptual proliferation regarding signs.

As for the statement that by skillfully cultivating this [non-conceptual knowledge], one attains the subsequently attained conventional knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-saṃvṛti-jñāna*) which is subsumed under it, and so forth:

The aforementioned conceptualization of discursive proliferation (*prapañca-saṃjñā*) is precisely what is termed conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) as post-attainment wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
According to this perspective, both the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) and the stage of Buddhahood possess conventional knowledge.
Therefore, it was stated above that the ten powers of the Buddhas are subsumed under conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*),
because they are accompanied by conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). Furthermore, another interpretation is as follows:
Conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is of two kinds:
first, that which is contaminated (*sāsrava*) and takes conventional reality as its object;
second, that which is uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), which is designated by the name "conventional knowledge" from a conventional perspective.
Regarding the present analysis of conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) across the three time periods,
this is stated based on the perspective of that contaminated (*sāsrava*) conventional wisdom;
it does not imply that the Tathāgata’s subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) is a contaminated conventional wisdom.
Xuán says: Here,
"reaching the ultimate stage" refers exclusively to the tenth bhūmi,
because it subsequently clarifies the three temporal dimensions of supramundane reality.

As for the statement that "the dharma-knowledge category of the path of seeing serves as the antidote to the afflictions of the desire realm to be abandoned through seeing," this is spoken of in a conventional sense and does not refer to the actual path of abandonment.
It is only when one cultivates the contemplation of true suchness within the state of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñi*) that one is able to abandon the afflictions.
Regarding the question, "When all types of subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) manifest, do they all comprehend the form and formless realms?
and so forth, the Supplement (Pū-chüeh) states:
This question concerns subsequent knowledge in its many various forms.
This refers to the path of preparation up to the path of advancement.
Prior to the path of seeing the unknown (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), the knowledge that contemplates the higher realms is termed "subsequent knowledge" (*anvaya-jñāna*).
Does it also clearly discern the form and formless realms?

The answer is: Within the path of insight (darśanamārga) of the mental aspect, all subsequent knowledges (anvayajñāna) are able to discern [their objects] because they have previously been well-cultivated through hearing and reflection;
others, however, cannot.
Furthermore, regarding all subsequent cognitions (anvaya-jñāna) prior to the Path of Seeing,
one cannot discern them at the initial contemplation;
however, if one has long engaged in hearing and reflection, one can indeed distinguish them.
Tài said: "If,

within the realm of form (rūpadhātu), one is to attain the wisdom resulting from reflection (cintāmayī-prajñā) and give rise to the wisdom resulting from cultivation (bhāvanāmayī-prajñā) by correctly grasping the signs,
then after having comprehensively understood them through the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) and the contemplation of the truths, one subsequently knows them individually."
If it were not so, one would merely understand the general observation and would be unable to achieve thorough knowledge.
Xuánzàng says:

The meaning of the question is whether one takes only sentient beings as the object, or whether one takes both the world of sentient beings (*sattvaloka*) and the physical world (*bhājanaloka*) as the objects.
In the response, two meanings may be discerned.
Regarding the statement that "the remaining various knowledges are subsumed under two categories," the Supplement (Bǔquè) says:
This refers to the knowledge of the Four Truths that penetrates both the dharma and its inference; its essence is *vipaśyanā*, which is concentration and wisdom (*samādhi-prajñā*).
Because it is characterized by tranquility, it is called *śamatha*.
As Xuánzàng says:
Because the eight patiences involve seeking, they are said to belong to the category of vipaśyanā;
because the eight knowledges involve the cessation of seeking, they are said to belong to the category of śamatha.
These are the various knowledges subsumed within these eight patiences and eight knowledges.
Regarding the statement that they are subsumed under the two categories of dharma and anvaya:
furthermore, as for those [seeds] that reach the stage of sequential manifestation during the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*),
the seeds of the path of seeing— which have existed from the beginning— cannot increase so long as they have not encountered superior conditions.
Now, the first moment of the path of insight (darśanamārga) characterized by signlessness (animitta) manifests;
it is able to universally permeate and activate all seeds of the path of insight, causing them to increase instantaneously—this is termed "attainment.
Thereafter, they gradually manifest in successive order.

The statement, "Because one correctly grasps the characteristics through the perception of characteristics regarding the various truths," explains the presence of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
The statement, "In order to cultivate sublime wisdom as it was previously seen and known," explains the transcendence of conceptual proliferation.
The phrase "in order to cause the mind to become weary through the practice of weariness with all worldly virtues" is a further explanation of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
The phrase "in order to experience the various delights of the sublime Dharma" is a further explanation of the supramundane wisdom that transcends conceptual proliferation.
Seventh, the distinctions of the attainments of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are clarified.
Regarding the phrase "such as King Mandhātṛ" and so forth: *Mandha* means "I" (*aham*) in this language;
*dhātṛ* means "nourisher" (*poṣaka*). Thus, it signifies one who nourishes the self.
Some say he was "Holding" (Chi),
while others say he was "Nurturing" (Yang); this refers to King Mūrdhaja.
His father was originally born upon his shoulder.
Upon that shoulder, a fetus grew on the crown of the king’s head;
later, it moved to his buttocks.
When the womb opened, there was a boy of extraordinary beauty;
the King took him onto his shoulders and brought him into the inner palace.
The king had one hundred wives.
The king asked, "Who among you can take care of this child?
They all knelt with their right knees on the ground and said, "I can take care of and nourish him."
The king then entrusted him to the first consort to raise him;
hence he received this name.
In this region, "Top-Born" (Mūrdhaja) is a name established based on his birth.
This is not the original, correct terminology.
Regarding such things as creating illusions, sorcery, or raising the dead through incantations, the Tripiṭaka states:
"In the West, there are people who, by means of the power of mantras or the power of illusion..."
If one causes that corpse to go to another location, engage in speech and dialogue, and return to its original place,
it is called a "fully risen corpse" (kṛtsna-vetāla).
If, however, one merely causes it to rise, sit, and respond to people, but cannot cause it to travel to another location, [it is not so called].
This is called "Half-Rising Corpse.
Tai says: "Furthermore, it is explained as follows."
If one can merely cause the tongue to protrude, it is called a "half-raised corpse.
This is as described in the tradition of Western incantation methods:
if one recites a spell over a corpse, its tongue will protrude.
One who obtains its tongue can obtain the Rain Sword.
One who obtains this sword ascends into the void and is able to go to the abodes of the various seers.
Its corpse constitutes the supreme whole.
Now, I shall further cite the *Vinaya-vibhāṣā* of the Sarvāstivāda school,
as recorded previously in the fifty-ninth fascicle.
Second, the explanation of the dharmas that are cognized.
In the first part of the middle section, five gates are opened and then explained according to those gates.
Within the explanation of the fifth gate, there is first an analysis of the obstacles and their remedies;
next, an analysis of the distinctions among the various mental characteristics; and finally, a summary.
Regarding the distinction in the arising [of states],

it is said that if one has not previously given rise to dhyāna or the formless attainments, when they first arise in the desire realm, the wholesome mind of the first dhyāna must necessarily arise immediately after a wholesome mind of the desire realm.
According to the *Abhidharmakośa*, it is taught that only from volition and wisdom associated with equanimity (*upekṣā*) within the desire realm can the mind of the form realm arise.
In the Mahāyāna, however, no such established text has been seen.
From the perspective of its meaning, minds associated with joy (*prīti*) and equanimity can both give rise to the concentrated mind (*samāhita-citta*).
It may also be inferred that the mind associated with equanimity (*upekṣā*) gives rise to the meditative mind (*samāhita-citta*),
because joy (*prīti*) is coarse and agitated, thereby obstructing meditative concentration.
According to the text of the *Maulī Bhūmi*, the latter interpretation is superior.
Furthermore, when one wishes for a wholesome mind to arise immediately after [the access concentration],
and subsequently enters the fundamental dhyāna because they share the same bond (ekabandhana),
it is therefore called the "mind of the first dhyāna."

Regarding the statement that "furthermore, from an indeterminate mind of the desire realm, a wholesome mind of the form realm arises immediately thereafter, because it does not arise from its own nature":
this mind of transformation is the fruit of dhyāna.
Therefore, it shares the same stage as dhyāna and is not bound to the desire realm.

Now, when one says "desire realm," it refers to the consciousness that takes the body of the desire realm as its object and perceives the images of the four sensory objects manifested through the transformations of the desire realm.
Why is this so? It is like when a mind of transformation belonging to the form realm performs the work of transformation in the desire realm.
The objects of transformation in the desire realm do not deviate;
they merely take as their object the four types of objects within the *nimittabhāga* (objective aspect) of one's own mind.
These are the images of the four objects of the desire realm.
That which resembles the four objects (*viṣaya*) of the desire realm is called "conditioned by the desire realm.

This means that the mind of transformation (*nirmāṇacitta*) is said to be "bound to the desire realm" (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) by virtue of its object of perception, not by its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
This differs from the Small Treatises (*Hīnayāna śāstras*), which hold that the mind of transformation belonging to the four dhyānas of the desire realm is itself subsumed under the desire realm.

Regarding the statement, "Furthermore, when one passes away from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and is born in a higher plane, a defiled mind of the higher plane arises immediately after a wholesome or neutral mind of the desire realm," this refers to the moment of death when one is about to pass away from the desire realm and is on the verge of being born in a higher plane.
Immediately following a wholesome mind or an indeterminate mind of the desire realm, according to the place where one is born,
a defiled mind of a higher plane arises at the time of death to moisten birth on that higher plane;
[one then passes away] from that defiled mind of a higher plane.
One also dies with the arising of a resultant indeterminate mind of the desire realm;
furthermore, the minds of the higher stages that arise are necessarily produced only within the sphere of activity belonging to their own respective stage.
Regarding the different treatises on the three natures at the moment of death:

as for the statement that "when one passes away from a higher plane and is reborn in a lower plane, immediately after any wholesome, defiled, or neutral mind of all higher planes, only a defiled mind of the lower plane arises," and so forth.
According to the principle of concomitant transformation (*anuvartana*),
when one passes away from a higher plane and is reborn in a lower plane,
although the body belongs to the higher plane, one does not give rise to a defiled mind of the lower plane.
Now, according to the gateway of ultimate reality,
when one whose body is in a higher realm is about to die,
they give rise to a defiled mind of a lower realm to moisten rebirth.
That defiled mind necessarily gives rise to a specific differentiation toward an object produced within its own stage (*svabhūmi*).
*Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra-vivaraṇa*, Fascicle 18, Part 2, End.
